title: Lab 4 - Digital Audio
text: In this lab I will use the MCU to play music by using timers to generate square waves and toggling a GPIO pin at a specific frequency for specified durations.

title: Lab 4 - Digital Audio
text:
Technical Documentation
The source code for the project can be found in the associated Github repository

Schematic



Schematic of the Design




Calculations
A timer is a counter that ticks up at a steady rate, and when it reaches a set limit it goes back to zero. Each wrap is one “cycle.” The prescaler and auto-reload value together determine how fast that happens. The prescaler slows the incoming 80 MHz clock down, so the counter only ticks once every so many clock pulses. The auto-reload value sets how many ticks the counter counts before wrapping.
For note duration I used TIM15. I set the prescaler to 79, so the counter ticks once every 80 clock pulses, which is 1 million ticks per second, or one tick per microsecond. I set the auto-reloadlimit to 999, so the counter counts 1000 ticks (1000 microseconds or 1 millisecond) and before resetting to zero.
delay_ms just waits for the timer to announce a wrap and counts them. A 125 ms note means waiting for 125 wraps. So note length in milliseconds equals the number of wraps you wait for.
To get the the pitches I usedTIM16. The timer generates a square wave (PWM) to produce the sound. The output pin is high for the first half of each cycle and low for the second half, which makes a square wave. The pitch that you hear is how many of these cycles happen per second.
 
Checking at 220 Hz and 1000 Hz is not sufficient to prove that all notes are within error bounds. This is because most of the error comes from the fact that the prescaler and auto-reload values are integers, and desired frequencies are not all exactly integers.

title: Lab 4 - Digital Audio

Conclusion
I spent about twelve hours working on this lab.

title: Lab 4 - Digital Audio
text:
AI Prototype Summary
I asked Gemini “What timers should I use on the STM32L432KC to generate frequencies ranging from 220Hz to 1kHz? What’s the best choice of timer if I want to easily connect it to a GPIO pin? What formulae are relevant, and what registers need to be set to configure them properly?”
It gave the following response: “To generate audio frequencies from 220Hz (A3 note) to 1kHz on the STM32L432KC (commonly found on the Nucleo-32 board), general-purpose timers TIM2, TIM15, or TIM16 are ideal choices.”
It also provided guidance on why these timers are suitable with governing calculations for frequency. I used TIM15 and TIM16, but I was surprised that these were the ones recommended since the I heard more often that using TIM6 and TIM7 was more efficient for this lab. I think AI can be helpful to guide the selection of timers as it can quickly synthesize information that is otherwise scattered across datasheets and reference manuals.

title: Lab 2 - Multiplexed 7-Segment Display
text: This lab can be split into two main parts. First, I designed a system to time multiplex a dual seven-segment display to show a 2-digit hexadecimal number. The second part of the lab was to design a keypad scanner that blinks an LED based on the column of the currently pressed key.

title: Lab 2 - Multiplexed 7-Segment Display
text: This lab can be split into two main parts. First, I designed a system to time multiplex a dual seven-segment display to show a 2-digit hexadecimal number. The second part of the lab was to design a keypad scanner that blinks an LED based on the column of the currently pressed key.

title: Lab 2 - Multiplexed 7-Segment Display
text:
Design and Testing Methodology

Frequency Calculations
For the first step of the design, the time multiplexing of the dual seven-segment display, I started with the seven segment decoder module I developed in the previous lab. I then had to find the correct frequency to multiplex the two displays. I looked online for what frequency the human eye can perceive as a constant light and found that it is around 60 Hz. I then decided to use a frequency of 120 Hz to multiplex the two displays to ensure there was no visible flicker. To achieve this frequency I used the on-board high-speed oscillator to generate a 48 MHz clock signal, then a counter was used with a max count of 200000 to generate a 120 Hz multiplexing frequency. My math to get the maximum count of 200000 is as follows: \(maxCount = \frac{48\text{ MHz}}{2 \times 120\text{ Hz}} = 200,000\)
Similar math was done to achieve the proper frequency for the keypad scanner. I wanted all 4 columns to be illuminated once within 0.5s. In other words, each LED should be on for 0.125 s in the scan pattern and the full scan pattern should complete twice within 1 second. In other words, you are scanning the full keypad twice per second (2 Hz). \(maxCount = {48\text{ MHz}} {\times 0.125\text{ s}} = 6,000,000\)


Hardware Design
The pinout schematic for the time-multiplexed dual seven-segment display is shown below. 2N3906 PNP transistors were used to drive the common anode of each display. I needed a resistor to limit the current through the base of the PNP transistor. The emitter is connected to 3.3 V. The base-emitter voltage drop is 0.65 V (from the datasheet), so the voltage at the base is then 2.65 V. The FPGA pins can handle a maximum current of 8 mA, so the base resistor should be at least 330 ohms to limit the current to a safe value. I chose to use a 1k ohm resistor to be safe.
For the resistors from the display cathodes to the FPGA pins, I used 150 ohm resistors. I got this by looking at the datasheet for the transistor and getting the Collector−Emitter Saturation Voltage of ~0.2V. This leaves the voltage at the collector to be about 3.1 V. This path eventually leads to an FPGA pin so the current cannot exceed 8 mA. The forward voltage of the LED segment is about 1.8 V for 8 mA of current. Calculations are shown below: 
The schematic is shown below. 
The schematic for the keypad scanner is also shown below. The rows of the keypad are connected to the FPGA pins through 2N3904 NPN transistors, and the columns of the keypad are connected to the FPGA pins directly. Internal 100k ohm pull-up resistors are used on the column pins. The LEDs are connected to the FPGA pin through 330 ohm resistors. These were chosen to limit the current through the LEDs. Using a typical forward voltage for a green LED of 2.1 V, the resistor will have 1.2 V across it. To keep the current within the FPGA’s and the LED’s constraints, I choose to use 330 ohm resistors which gives a current of 3.6 mA. This is well within the range.

title: Lab 1 - FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text: In this lab, a design was implemented on the FPGA to program a seven segment display, to show hexadecimal digits from 0 to F given a binary input. Two LEDs were also programmed with set logic given the input, and a third LED was programmed to blink at 2.4 Hz.

title: Lab 1 - FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text: In this lab, a design was implemented on the FPGA to program a seven segment display, to show hexadecimal digits from 0 to F given a binary input. Two LEDs were also programmed with set logic given the input, and a third LED was programmed to blink at 2.4 Hz.

title: Lab 1 - FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text:
Design and Testing Methodology

Design Overview
The first step in the design was to determine the logic needed for the first two LEDs which resulted in a XOR gate and an AND gate. The third blinking LED utilized the on-board high-speed oscillator to generate a 48 MHz clock signal, then a counter was used at a cycle of 20000000 to generate a 2.4 Hz blinking frequency.
The second part of the design included the 7 segment display decoder module that mapped the binary input to the segments of the display that needed to be illuminated to display the correct hexadecimal digit.

title: Lab 1 - FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text:
Technical Documentation
The source code for the project can be found in the associated Github repository

Block Diagram



Figure 1: Block Diagram of the Design




Schematic



Figure 2: FPGA Output Pins and their Corresponding Display Pins




Resistor Calculations
To determine the appropriate resistor values, I used the forward voltage and current ratings from the 7-segment display datasheet. From the datasheet, I found that the voltage drop is typically 2.1 V, so with a 3.3 V supply voltage the resistor will have 1.2 V across it. To keep the current within the FPGA’s and the display’s constraints, I choose to use 150 ohm resistors which gives a current of 8 mA. This is well within the range.


Blink Frequency Calculations
The blink LED (led2) is driven by blinkCounter, clocked by the FPGA’s internal high speed oscillator (HSOSC) at \(f_{clk} = 48\text{ MHz}\). The counter increments once per clock cycle and toggles led2 every time it reaches DIV - 1 cycles. I calculated the value of DIV to achieve a blink frequency of 2.4 Hz as follows: \(DIV = \frac{48\text{ MHz}}{2 \times 2.4\text{ Hz}} = 10,000,000\)
48 MHz is the frequency of the internal oscillator, 2.4 Hz is the desired blink frequency, and the factor of 2 in the denominator accounts for the fact that the LED toggles on every other cycle of the counter. The resulting value of DIV is 10,000,000, which means that the counter will count to 10 million before toggling the LED, resulting in a blink frequency of 2.4 Hz.

Lab 5 - Interrupts
text: For this lab, I built a system to determine the angular velocity of a brushed DC motor using my MCU, a quadrature encoder, and a motor. I set up the MCU to use interrupts to detect pulses from the encoder and use them to calculate a direction and velocity. I ensured that the system remains functional when the motor is spinning at very high and very low speeds by changing the way I calculate velocity based on the time between encoder pulses. I display the direction and angular velocity of the motor in revolutions/s with an update rate of 1 Hz using printf.

title: Lab 5 - Interrupts
text: For this lab, I built a system to determine the angular velocity of a brushed DC motor using my MCU, a quadrature encoder, and a motor. I set up the MCU to use interrupts to detect pulses from the encoder and use them to calculate a direction and velocity. I ensured that the system remains functional when the motor is spinning at very high and very low speeds by changing the way I calculate velocity based on the time between encoder pulses. I display the direction and angular velocity of the motor in revolutions/s with an update rate of 1 Hz using printf.

title: Lab 5 - Interrupts
text:
Technical Documentation
The source code for the project can be found in the associated Github repository

title: Lab 5 - Interrupts
text:
Calculations

Converting encoder pulses to velocity and direction
The encoder has two Hall-effect channels, A and B, 90° out of phase. The Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) triggers on both the rising and falling edges of both channels.
The ISR reads both pins at once and forms a 2-bit state, (A << 1) | B. In one direction the state sequence is 00 → 01 → 11 → 10 → 00, and in the other it runs in reverse. The ISR looks up the (previous state, current state) pair in a 16-entry table where one step forward gives +1,one step backward gives −1, and no change (or a 2-bit jump) gives 0.
The ISR adds the result to a signed count, so the count increases in one direction and decreases in the other. The sign of the velocity comes from the sign of the count change. A positive change is displayed as CW, and a negative change is displayed as CCW (when looking down at the spinning shaft).
On each valid edge the ISR records a timestamp from TIM2 and the number of ticks since the previous valid edge. The counter wraps only every 2³² µs ≈ 71.6 minutes. This is a pretty long amount of time and why I wanted to use the 32-bit counter.
The main loop takes a snapshot of the count, last-edge time, last interval, and direction, with interrupts briefly disabled while it samples so we don’t get any weird values. It then uses one of three methods to calculate the velocity. I implemented this 3 method approach to ensure the reading was accurate across a wide range of motor speeds. The three methods are described below.



Three Calculation Methods (Only one is ever used at a time)



Window Method
The window method is used for faster speeds (>= 50 counts). T_window is the measured time between snapshots in ticks, not an assumed 1 s, so the result stays correct if the loop runs slightly long.


Period Method
The period method is used for slow speeds. If fewer than 50 counts arrived and an edge occurred within the last 2 s then the velocity is calculated using the last interval between edges. Δt is the larger of the last interval and the time since the last edge. Using the time since the last edge helps get low-speed readings more accurately.


Zero Method
The last method just outputs zero velocity. If there is no valid interval yet or no edge in the last 2 seconds, the speed is reported as 0.



Update Rate and Resolution
The update rate is set by the update period of 1 s, declared at the top of main.c as UPDATE_PERIOD_TICKS. So the update rate is 1 Hz. The loop stores the time of each update before it calls printf, so print time does not lengthen the period. The speed calculation also divides by the measured number of timer ticks between updates instead of assuming exactly 1 s, so a slightly late update does not change anything.
The resolution of the velocity output depends on the method used to calculate the speed:
Window method (50 or more counts per update). The speed is the net count change divided by the counts per revolution and the window length. The count is an integer, so the speed can only change in steps of one count:
\[\Delta\omega = \frac{1}{\text{CPR} \cdot T_u} = \frac{1}{1632 \times 1\ \text{s}} = 6.13 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{rev/s}\]
At the nominal speed of 2.825 rev/s, the window holds about \(1632 \times 2.825 \approx 4610\) counts, so one count of uncertainty is \(1/4610 \approx 0.022\%\). The timer contributes much less: the 1 MHz timestamp adds at most \(\pm 1\ \mu\text{s}\) in a 1,000,000 µs window, which is \(0.0001\%\), so the count dominates the error.
Period method (fewer than 50 counts per update). The speed is computed from the time \(\Delta t\) for a single step. Here the error comes from the 1 µs timer tick, so the relative error is \(1\ \mu\text{s} / \Delta t\). This method is used only below the switching speed, so its worst case is there. At 50 counts per update, \(\Delta t = 20\ \text{ms}\), giving about 0.005%, and the error shrinks further as the motor slows and the interval grows.
Zero speed. If no edge arrives for 2 s, or none has arrived yet, the speed is reported as zero. This sets the slowest nonzero speed the system can report to be
\[\omega_{min} = \frac{1}{\text{CPR} \cdot T_0} = \frac{1}{1632 \times 2\ \text{s}} = 3.06 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{rev/s}\]


Measured vs. Calculated Velocity
Here, I verify the accuracy of my calculations to ensure that the my system is accurate. I got less than a 1% error at 12V so I am confident in my results.

title: Lab 5 - Interrupts
section: Discussion: Interrupt-based detection vs. manual polling
text:
Discussion: Interrupt-based detection vs. manual polling
Interrupts and polling do the same work per edge (read both pins, look up the step, update the count) but differ in how the CPU learns an edge occurred.
I redid my code to run with polling instead of interrupts and ran it. You can check out the code in my lab5 repository in polling_test.c. For 12 V I got a measured speed of 2.885 rev/s. This is a 2% error from the calculated speed of 2.825 rev/s. In comparison, the interrupt-based implementation measured 2.852 rev/s (<1% error), making polling over twice as inaccurate.
For polling, the CPU repeatedly checks a device’s status in a continuous loop to see if it needs attention. This is simple to implement but wastes processing power. In contrast, with interrupts, the CPU works simultaneously on other tasks until a device sends an active signal that it requires service, prompting the CPU to briefly pause its current work, execute an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR), and then resume where it left off.
The tradeoff for interrupts is added complexity in exchange for low CPU load, lossless counting while other code runs, and better timing accuracy, so interrupts are the better choice for this lab where the motor speed can change at any second and we want to constantly record values. Polling would make sense only for a dedicated, very high edge rate with nothing else running.

title: Lab 5 - Interrupts
text:
AI Prototype Summary
I asked Gemini: “Write me interrupt handlers to interface with a quadrature encoder. I’m using the STM32L432KC, what pins should I connect the encoder to in order to allow it to easily trigger the interrupts?”
It responded with “When interfacing a quadrature encoder with an STM32 micro, the most efficient approach is not to manually trigger GPIO interrupts (EXTI). Manual EXTI interrupts burn significant CPU cycles and risk missing steps at higher RPMs.
Instead, the STM32 contains dedicated hardware peripheral timer channels in Encoder Mode. The timer listens directly to channels TIMx_CH1 and TIMx_CH2, automatically decoding x2 or x4 quadrature signals and driving a hardware 16-bit or 32-bit counter up or down on its own without any CPU overhead.”
It gave me the choice to use Modern STM32 HAL Implementation (Hardware Encoder Mode) or Manual EXTI Interrupt Handlers, recommending the former for efficiency and reliability. I selected the first option as it recommended, and it gave me some weird things to set up I hadn’t really done before.
